                                         I. INTRODUCTION
        On May 15, 2026, Mark Friesenhahn filed his RFIs with Applicants. The Applicants’
objections were filed on May 22, 2026, under Control Number 59475 Item Number
5068. T h e A p p l i c a n t s s t a t e d t h a t M a r k F r i e s e n h a h n ’ s R F I Questions Nos.
01-10 and 01-11 seek information that is neither relevant nor calculated to lead to the
discovery of admissible evidence.

Mark Friesenhahn Request to Overrule Applicants Objection to Mark Friesenhahn’s First
Request for Information
                                                                                 1
        Accordingly, Applicants filed their Objections. The Applicants stated that “the Permian
Basin Reliability Plan ("PBRP") load forecasts were not based on attestation letters”, and that
“the PBRP import paths were selected to address ERCOT-wide electric demand and usage
patterns not the projected load growth of the Applicants or any single utility”. The Applicants
claimed that Mr. Friesenhahn is “seeking information that is neither relevant nor reasonably
calculated to lead to the discovery of admissible evidence.”

        Mark Friesenhahn firmly disagrees with this position and stated such during a telephone
conversation with LCRA Counsel outlined under NEGOTATIONS section below. Mr.
Friesenhahn feels that the load forecasts are based on not only the PBRP, but also the subsequent
2024 and 2025 Regional Transmission Plans issued in December 2024 and December 2025,
respectively.


                                          II. NEGOTIATIONS

         Christina, Counsel for Applicants, telephoned Mark Friesenhahn on 05/21/26 to discuss
his 59475 RFIs #10 and #11 and asked if he would consider modifying these RFIs.
         We discussed our individual views on the Permian Basin (PB) forecast that “supports” the
nominal 44 GW load forecast and justification for the proposed 765 kV powerlines.
         Mr. Friesenhahn noted that “clearly the three proposed powerlines would only handle
about 15 GW, leaving the need for significant power generation in the PB”. She had no comment
on this.
         Mr. Friesenhahn further stated that he feels “the attestation letters form the basis for
about 32 GW of power demand in the PB, and that in turn the attestation letters provide the
justification for the power lines proposed by the TSPs.”
         Mr. Friesenhahn also stated that he would be happy to accept a representative “cross-
section” of the attestation letters along with LCRA’s description of the process they and ONCOR
used to develop a conceptual estimate of 218 GW 1 demand from the attestation letters.
         Mr. Friesenhahn noted that ERCOT recognized the 218 GW was unrealistically high and
risked the number down to something like 27% of the 218 GW arriving at the 62 GW
(approximately ½ of this amount, 32 GW, is in the PB) number used in ERCOT’s RTP reports.
         Further, Mr. Friesenhahn has been involved professionally in numerous conceptual
planning studies on large projects where the cumulative early estimates need to be tempered to
realistically achievable values, timing constraints, etc. In addition, early conceptual cost
estimates are normally based on unit parameters from other projects and are generally low when
the project parameters are further defined. No question in his mind that the powerline costs will
probably at least double based on his experience..
         Mr. Friesenhahn feels that ERCOT’s 2024 and 2025 RTP reports cumulatively add to the
overall assessment of PB load forecast and thus are relevant and part of the overall review and
SOAH hearing process on the CCN amendments to add the proposed powerlines.


1
    2025 Regional Transmission Plan, December 2025, pg. 6.

Mark Friesenhahn Request to Overrule Applicants Objection to Mark Friesenhahn’s First
Request for Information
                                                                                 2
        Christina stated that LCRA believes that the attestation letters are “outside the scope” of
the hearings and are not included in the PBRP. LCRA will object and say so in response to Mr.
Friesenhahn’s views to the contrary on RFI Questions Nos. 01-10 and 01-11. Thus, they will not
provide the attestation letters.
       We had further productive discussion on the overall need for the powerlines and shared
contrasting views.
       Mr. Friesenhahn noted that he appreciated the dialogue to better understand each other
and our opposing views. He believes that effective problem solving begins with dialogue.

            III. SPECIFIC OBJECTIONS TO MARK FRIESENHAHN'S RFIs

       Applicants objected to the following RFIs:

       FRIESENHAHN 01-10

      Provide copies of all attestation letters that define the load forecast for each
customer that Oncor and LCRA TSP provided to ERCOT &/or PUC for their Dec 2024
and Dec 2025 Regional Transmission Plans.

       FRIESENHAHN 01-11

        Provide detailed information supporting the attestation Letters, including the basis
for the load estimate, assumptions provided by the potential customer and Oncor.

         Applicants objected to Question No. 01-10 because “the information sought is irrelevant.
The scope of permissible discovery is limited to information and documents that are relevant,
reasonably calculated to lead to the discovery of admissible evidence, and proportionate to the
needs of the case. 1 01-10 asks for copies of the attestation letters that define the load forecast
for each customer Oncor and LCRA provided to ERCOT and or the PUC." 01-11 asks the
Applicants to "provide detailed information supporting the attestation letter including the basis
for the load estimate and assumptions provided by the potential customer and the Applicants.
The Permian Basin Reliability Plan ("PBRP") load forecasts were not based on attestation
letters. Furthermore, the PBRP import paths were selected to address ERCOT-wide electric
demand and usage patterns, not the projected load growth of the Applicants or any single utility.
01-10 and 01-11 thus seek information that is neither relevant nor reasonably calculated to lead
to the discovery of admissible evidence. Accordingly, these requests exceed the scope of
permissible discovery.”

  IV. MARK FRIESENHAHN'S POSITION ON THESE RFIs (SUPPORTING HIS
REQUEST TO THE SOAH AJLS TO OVERRULE THE LCRA/ONCOR OBJECTIONS)

       Mark Friesenhahn firmly disagrees with the Applicant’s position and feels that the load
forecasts are based on not only the PBRP, but also the subsequent 2024 and 2025 Regional
Transmission Plans (RTPs) issued in December 2024 and December 2025, respectively. These


Mark Friesenhahn Request to Overrule Applicants Objection to Mark Friesenhahn’s First
Request for Information
                                                                                 3
 three reports must be taken cumulatively (together) to understand the basis of the Applicants’
load forecast that provide justification for the proposed powerlines.
        Mr. Friesenhahn notes that “Attestation Letters” were not part of the PBRP (as stated by
LCRA/Oncor) but were a significant component of the 2024 and 2025 RTP reports leading the
load forecast by TSPs.
        Specifically, the total load forecast data from all three reports must be considered to
understand the TSP position for developing their load forecast that supports their proposed
powerlines. Key points from these three reports are tabulated below to illustrate this. Attachment
1 includes more detailed excerpts from these reports for reference.

1. Requirements in the 2024 PBRP

   a. In 2023, the Texas Legislature enacted House Bill (HB) 5066, which, among other things,
       required the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) to direct ERCOT to develop a
       reliability plan for the Permian Basin region (PBRP). As required by HB 5066, ERCOT’s
       reliability plan for the Permian Basin must:
          i.Address extending transmission service to areas where mineral resources have been
                found;
         ii.Address increasing available capacity to meet forecasted load; and
        iii.Provide available infrastructure to reduce interconnection times in areas without
                access to transmission service.
   b. Data provided by TSPs—and relied upon by ERCOT for the purposes of this study, as
       required by statute indicates that the electric demand driven by oil and gas development
       in the Permian Basin is continuing to grow over the next 15 years.
    c. ……in addition to rapid growth in oil and natural gas demand, TDSPs have also
        provided demand projections indicating an exponential increase in the number of non-oil
        and gas loads in the Permian Basin region. The majority of the forecasted demand
        associated with these non-oil and gas loads primarily consists of demand related to
        cryptocurrency mining operations, data centers, and hydrogen electrolysis facilities.

2. Requirements in the 2024 Regional Transmission Plans (RTP)

   a. In December 2022, the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) amended 16 Texas
      Administrative Code (TAC) § 25.101 to implement Senate Bill (SB) 1281 (87th
      Legislature). The amendments included the requirement for any review conducted by
      ERCOT to incorporate historical load, forecasted load growth, and additional load
      currently seeking interconnection.
   b. In June 2023, House Bill (HB) 5066 (88th Legislature) was enacted, introducing a new
      requirement to consider loads for which the electric utility has yet to execute an
      interconnection agreement, as determined by the electric utility responsible for serving
      the load.
   c. These new requirements combined with unprecedented economic growth led to a
      significant increase in large loads considered in the 2024 RTP (i.e., data centers,
      hydrogen and hydrogen-related manufacturing, crypto mining, and electrification)

Request for Information
                                                                                 4
    d. The implementation of House Bill (HB) 5066 in 2024 RTP brought substantial changes
      into the planning process, moving the ERCOT region into a new era of planning.
   e. Prior to the 2024 RTP, ERCOT only considered those large loads that had an executed
      contract with their electric utility to determine the appropriate load to include in the
      analysis.
   f. HB 5066 introduced a new requirement to consider loads for which the electric utility has
      yet to sign an interconnection agreement, as determined by the electric utility responsible
      for serving the load. Consequently,
   g. ERCOT considered attestation letters from TSP officers to determine the appropriate load
      to include.

3. Requirements in the 2025 Regional Transmission Plans (RTP)

   a. The large loads submitted by TSPs for consideration under the HB5066 requirements in
      the 2025 RTP saw an even more significant increase compared to the 2024 RTP. The
      forecasted summer peak demand for 2031 would have exceeded 218 GW if all TSP-
      submitted large loads were included.
   b. After performing historical analysis on large load realization, ERCOT developed an
      ERCOT Transmission Planning Adjusted Load Forecast (ETPALF) which adjusted the
      2031 forecast to 159 GW.
   c. The ETPALF preserved large loads substantiated with an interconnection agreement at
      100%; large loads substantiated with officer attestations (“Officer Letter Loads” – OLLs)
      were reduced to 55.4%; and, data center OLLs were further reduced to 49.8% of the
      initial OLL reduction, resulting in a final amount that was 27.6% of the full data center
      value.
   d. The ETPALF methodology resulted in the incorporation of over 60 GW of large loads in
      the 2025 RTP. ERCOT requested a Good Cause Exception (GCE) from the PUCT to use
      the ETPALF in the 2025 RTP. The GCE was approved on June 5, 2025

                                        V. REQUEST

   With the above considerations and facts, Mark Friesenhahn requests that Your Honors
   overrule the Applicant’s Objections, and order Applicants to respond to Question No. 01-10
   and 01-11, and thus satisfy Mark Friesenhahn’s request for the specific information outlined
   in these RFIs.

Request for Information

                                                  Attachment 1

       Included below are excerpts from ERCOT Permian Basin Reliability Plan Study, Final,
July 2024, 2024 Regional Transmission Plan, December 2024; and 2025 Regional Transmission
Plan, December 2025.

        These excerpts support Mark Friesenhahn’s position that the load forecasts are based on
not only the PBRP, but also the subsequent 2024 and 2025 Regional Transmission Plans (RTPs)
issued in December 2024 and December 2025, respectively. These three reports must be taken
cumulatively to understand the basis of the Applicants’ load forecast that provide justification for
the proposed powerlines. It is noted that “Attestation Letters” were not part of the PBRP but
were a significant component of the 2024 and 2025 RTP reports leading the load forecast by
TSPs. Excerpts include footnote citations as to location of the excerpts in the reports.

           Excerpts from ERCOT Permian Basin Reliability Plan Study, Final, July 2024

         In 2023, the Texas Legislature enacted House Bill (HB) 5066, which, among other things,
required the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) to direct ERCOT to develop a
reliability plan for the Permian Basin region.1 As required by HB 5066, ERCOT’s reliability plan
for the Permian Basin must2:
              Address extending transmission service to areas where mineral resources have
                 been found;
              Address increasing available capacity to meet forecasted load; and
              Provide available infrastructure to reduce interconnection times in areas without
                 access to transmission service.

         While the Permian Basin has already experienced unprecedented load growth, data
provided by TDSPs—and relied upon by ERCOT for the purposes of this study, as required by
statute indicates that the electric demand driven by oil and gas development in the Permian Basin
is continuing to grow over the next 15 years. Specifically, a 2022 load forecast developed by
S&P Global and submitted to ERCOT by Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (Oncor)
projected growth in peak oil-and-gas- related demand of 11,964 MW in 2030 and 14,705 MW in
2039, reflecting an expectation of a material expansion of oil and gas development in the
Permian Basin region.

        However, in addition to rapid growth in oil and natural gas demand, TDSPs have also
provided demand projections indicating an exponential increase in the number of non-oil and gas
loads in the Permian Basin region. The majority of the forecasted demand associated with these
non-oil and gas loads primarily consists of demand related to cryptocurrency mining operations,
data centers, and hydrogen electrolysis facilities. The total additional non-oil-and-gas demand in
the Permian Basin region for 2030 (and 2038) based on information provided by the TDSPs is
2
    ERCOT Permian Basin Reliability Plan Study, Final, July 2024, pg. ii

Request for Information
                                                                                 6
 11,695 MW. Summing the S&P Global forecast with the TDSP-provided load forecasts, the total
demand in the Permian Basin region ERCOT has modeled in its studies for 2030 is 23,659 MW,
and the total demand modeled for 2038 is 26,400 MW. 3


           Excerpts from ERCOT 2024 Regional Transmission Plan, December 2024

         As the new load interconnection timeline outpaces the development of transmission
projects, the Texas Legislature recognized the need to update rules in the ERCOT Region.
Previously, these rules did not allow ERCOT to include loads in planning studies unless they had
executed an interconnection agreement. Updating these rules is essential to expedite the process
in order to reliably serve the anticipated rapid demand growth. In December 2022, the Public
Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) amended 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) § 25.101 to
implement Senate Bill (SB) 1281 (87th Legislature). The amendments included the requirement
for any review conducted by ERCOT to incorporate historical load, forecasted load growth, and
additional load currently seeking interconnection. In June 2023, House Bill (HB) 5066 (88th
Legislature) was enacted, introducing a new requirement to consider loads for which the electric
utility has yet to execute an interconnection agreement, as determined by the electric utility
responsible for serving the load.
         These new requirements combined with unprecedented economic growth led to a
significant increase in large loads considered in the 2024 RTP (i.e., data centers, hydrogen and
hydrogen-related manufacturing, crypto mining, and electrification). The forecasted summer
peak demand for 2030 exceeded 150 GW, of which approximately 50 GW is large load. Close to
40 GW of that forecasted demand for large loads seeking interconnections is due to the new rules
permitting additional forms of Substantiated Load beyond just load with an executed
interconnection agreement.


        In addition to the magnitude of the load growth, the “flat” or constant nature of the large
loads adds another layer of complexity. Most of the large loads seeking interconnection are
expected to maintain consistent electricity consumption regardless of season, day, or time.
Ensuring reliable interconnection for these loads requires a resource mix capable of supporting
their 24/7 demand. According to the capacity expansion results from the 2024 ERCOT Long-
Term System Assessment (LTSA) high large load adoption scenario, this resource mix requires
additional dispatchable Generation Resources. 4


        The implementation of House Bill (HB) 5066 in the 2024 RTP brought substantial
changes into the planning process, moving the ERCOT region into a new era of planning. Prior
to the 2024 RTP, ERCOT only considered those large loads that had an executed contract with
their electric utility to determine the appropriate load to include in the analysis. This resulted in
the inclusion of approximately 8 GW of large loads in both the 2022 and 2023 RTPs. HB5066

 introduced a new requirement to consider loads for which the electric utility has yet to sign an
interconnection agreement, as determined by the electric utility responsible for serving the load.
Consequently, ERCOT considered attestation letters from TSP officers to determine the
appropriate load to include. With both signed contracts and TSP officer letters considered, the
large load incorporated in the 2024 RTP exceeded 50 GW.5

      These large loads include cryptocurrency load, data center load, and hydrogen and
hydrogen-related manufacturing.


          Excerpts from ERCOT 2025 Regional Transmission Plan, December 2025

        House Bill (HB) 5066 (88th Legislative Session) introduced a new requirement to
consider loads for which the electric utility has yet to sign an interconnection agreement, as
determined by the electric utility responsible for serving the load. Consequently, ERCOT
accepted attestation letters from TSP officers (“Officer Letters”) as substantiation for inclusion in
the analysis. These new requirements were first implemented in the 2024 RTP and led to a
significant increase in large loads included in that assessment (i.e., data centers, crypto mining,
hydrogen and hydrogen-related manufacturing, and electrification). In the 2024 RTP, the
forecasted summer peak demand for 2030 exceeded 150 gigawatts (GW), with close to 40 GW
attributed to large loads seeking interconnections under the new requirements.

         The large loads submitted by TSPs for consideration under the HB 5066 requirements in
the 2025 RTP saw an even more significant increase compared to the 2024 RTP. The forecasted
summer peak demand for 2031 would have exceeded 218 GW if all TSP-submitted large loads
were included. After performing historical analysis on large load realization, ERCOT developed
an ERCOT Transmission Planning Adjusted Load Forecast (ETPALF) which adjusted the 2031
forecast to 159 GW. The ETPALF preserved large loads substantiated with an interconnection
agreement at 100%; large loads substantiated with officer attestations (“Officer Letter Loads” –
OLLs) were reduced to 55.4%; and, data center OLLs were further reduced to 49.8% of the
initial OLL reduction, resulting in a final amount that was 27.6% of the full data center value.
The ETPALF methodology resulted in the incorporation of over 60 GW of large loads in the
2025 RTP. ERCOT requested a Good Cause Exception (GCE) from the PUCT to use the
ETPALF in the 2025 RTP. The GCE was approved on June 5, 2025 6.

required the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) to direct ERCOT to develop a
reliability plan for the Permian Basin region.1 As required by HB 5066, ERCOT's reliability plan
for the Permian Basin must2:
             • Address extending transmission service to areas where mineral resources have
                 been found;
             • Address increasing available capacity to meet forecasted load; and

         While the Permian Basin has already experienced unprecedented load growth, data
provided by TDSPs-and relied upon by ERCOT for the purposes of this study, as required by

is continuing to grow over the next 15 years. Specifically, a 2022 load forecast developed by
S&P Global and submitted to ERCOT by Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (Oncor)
projected growth in peak oil-and-gas- related demand of 11,964 MW in 2030 and 14,705 MW in
2039, reflecting an expectation of a material expansion of oil and gas development in the
Permian Basin region.

loads in the Permian Basin region. The majority of the forecasted demand associated with these
non-oil and gas loads primarily consists of demand related to cryptocurrency mining operations,
data centers, and hydrogen electrolysis facilities. The total additional non-oil-and-gas demand in
the Permian Basin region for 2030 (and 2038) based on information provided by the TDSPs is

        Excerpts from ERCOT 2024 Regional Transmission Plan, December 2024

         As the new load interconnection timeline outpaces the development of transmission
projects, the Texas Legislature recognized the need to update rules in the ERCOT Region.
Previously, these rules did not allow ERCOT to include loads in planning studies unless they had
executed an interconnection agreement. Updating these rules is essential to expedite the process
in order to reliably serve the anticipated rapid demand growth. In December 2022, the Public
Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) amended 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) § 25.101 to
implement Senate Bill (SB) 1281 (87th Legislature). The amendments included the requirement
for any review conducted by ERCOT to incorporate historical load, forecasted load growth, and
additional load currently seeking interconnection. In June 2023, House Bill (HB) 5066 (88th
Legislature) was enacted, introducing a new requirement to consider loads for which the electric
utility has yet to execute an interconnection agreement, as determined by the electric utility
responsible for serving the load.
         These new requirements combined with unprecedented economic growth led to a
significant increase in large loads considered in the 2024 RTP (i.e., data centers, hydrogen and
hydrogen-related manufacturing, crypto mining, and electrification). The forecasted summer
peak demand for 2030 exceeded 150 GW, of which approximately 50 GW is large load. Close to
40 GW of that forecasted demand for large loads seeking interconnections is due to the new rules
permitting additional forms of Substantiated Load beyond just load with an executed
interconnection agreement.


       In addition to the magnitude of the load growth, the "flaf' or constant nature of the large
loads adds another layer of complexity. Most of the large loads seeking interconnection are
expected to maintain consistent electricity consumption regardless of season, day, or time.
Ensuring reliable interconnection for these loads requires a resource mix capable of supporting
their 24/7 demand. According to the capacity expansion results from the 2024 ERCOT Long-
Term System Assessment (LTSA) high large load adoption scenario, this resource mix requires
additional dispatchable Generation Resources. 4


        The implementation of House Bill (HB) 5066 in the 2024 RTP brought substantial
changes into the planning process, moving the ERCOT region into a new era of planning. Prior
to the 2024 RTP, ERCOT only considered those large loads that had an executed contract with
their electric utility to determine the appropriate load to include in the analysis. This resulted in
the inclusion of approximately 8 GW of large loads in both the 2022 and 2023 RTPs. HB5066

consider loads for which the electric utility has yet to sign an interconnection agreement, as
determined by the electric utility responsible for serving the load. Consequently, ERCOT

significant increase in large loads included in that assessment (i.e., data centers, crypto mining,
hydrogen and hydrogen-related manufacturing, and electrification). In the 2024 RTP, the
forecasted summer peak demand for 2030 exceeded 150 gigawatts (GW), with close to 40 GW
attributed to large loads seeking interconnections under the new requirements.

OLLs) were reduced to 55.4%; and, data center OLLs were further reduced to 49.8% of the
initial OLL reduction, resulting in a final amount that was 27.6% of the full data center value.
